chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: PRINCIPLE

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: Actigraphy involves the direct measurement of movement and indirect assessment of sleep using specific algorithms. During sleep, there is little movement, whereas a periodic increase in movement occurs during wake. Movement is sampled many times each second, and this is usually stored in epochs of 1 minute duration. The data thus obtained are viewed in the software, checked for errors, and then analyzed to determine whether the subject is in sleep or wake. The data is digitized by the software and scored as wake/sleep by automated computer algorithms that can vary depending on the manufacturer/ software.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: Digitization of data can be done by three methods: (1) time above threshold (TAT), which uses the duration that the activity crosses a defned threshold in each epoch; (2) zero crossing mode (ZCM), which measures the number of times the signal crosses zero in each epoch; and (3) digital integration mode (DIM), which computes the area under the curve. Some actigraphs can use more than one of these methods.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: Sleep estimation algorithms, also called sleep scoring functions, use the movement data

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: collected by the actigraph (activity counts) during each 1 minute epoch and transforms it into a sleep score, which can have a binary value of 0 (wake) or 1 (sleep). Various validated sleep estimation algorithms depend on factors like the make of the device, age of study population, epoch length, etc. The Cole–Kripke algorithm and the University of California, San Diego (UCSD) scoring algorithm are commonly used algorithms.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: Te following are the common parameters obtained from the data:

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report

text: PROCEDURE

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: Before the Test

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: Before the test, a complete history should be taken, and a physical examination of the patient should be carried out. Te history should include sleep history, medication history, and history of any past or present injury/illness. In addition, sleep questionnaires can be used to aid in the assessment of sleep.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: Te test procedure should be explained to the patient, and an informed consent should be taken. Te patient should also be educated about the do’s and don’ts and precautions in advance.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: Te Actigraph battery should be kept fully charged in advance. Following this, the actigraph must be set up to initialize data collection. For this, the device is connected to a computer usually via USB or Bluetooth. In the sofware provided by the manufacturer, the various study parameters and patient particulars are entered. Tis includes the start and end times for the data collection. Recording is usually carried out for a duration of 7–14 days as both weekday and weekend sleep patterns can be obtained. Te data collection can be started immediately or at a specifed time in the future. Tis helps in conserving battery life and storage of the device.

text: ● Te subject should be instructed to not get the device wet if it is not water resistant. To be on the safe side, the instrument should be kept from being wet even if it is water resistant.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: Te patient wears the device, usually on the nondominant wrist, and starts the recording on the device. In infants and toddlers, the actigraph is usually attached to the ankle. Te device should ft snugly and should be neither too loose nor too tight.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: Te patient is also asked to keep a sleep diary for the duration of the study. Te following events should be mentioned in the sleep diary (details on how to complete a sleep diary are given in Chapter 17):

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ● Time that the actigraph was removed and worn again

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ● Any other situations that could have interfered with sleep—illness, travel, etc.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: In addition, the subject is instructed to press the event marker button on the actigraph during any nighttime awakenings in addition to the events just listed.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: Precautions

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ● Te battery should be fully charged in advance and checked before initializing the recording.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ● If the recording duration is more than a week, the data can be downloaded every week to prevent loss of data in case a battery problem is suspected.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ● For devices with a light sensor, the subject should be instructed to ensure that it is not covered by the sleeve or any part of clothing.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ● Te device and sensors should be checked peri­

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: odically to determine if calibration is required.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ● If the subject’s skin is sensitive, the actigraph can be taken of for a short duration daily to avoid pressure sores. Te same is logged in the sleep diary.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ● If the device is removed during the duration of the recording, the subject is instructed to put it back on the same wrist.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: Te actigraphy recording can be uploaded and viewed on a laptop or computer immediately afer the actigraph is taken of the wrist. Te sleep diary, along with event markers, are used to aid in editing the data. Data corresponding to periods toward the start and fnish of the recording when the actigraph was not worn by the subject are deleted. If the device has been removed for any activity, e.g., bathing, exercise, etc., and the same is mentioned in the sleep diary, the period is manually scored as wake. In case of any uncertainty, the period should be marked as missing data or deleted to prevent it from being automatically scored as sleep. Also look for any aberrant movements in the recording, which should raise suspicion of a device error. In that case, the corresponding part of the data should be omitted from the analysis.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: Te actigraph usually comes with sofware that can be used for scoring rest/activity and identifying the status as sleep or wake. One such actigraphy template represented pictorially is shown in

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: EVIDENCE

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: Te American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) releases clinical practice guidelines on the use of actigraphy in sleep disorders based on available evidence. Te recommendations are classifed as Strong and Conditional. Strong recommendations are meant to be followed for most patients, while Conditional recommendations should be implemented based on clinical judgment on a case-tocase basis.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: Studies have compared actigraphy against polysomnography (PSG), which is considered the gold standard in sleep assessment. In individuals who do not have any sleep abnormalities, the total duration of sleep obtained using actigraphy had good correlation when compared to polysomnography.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: Actigraphy estimates of sleep efciency and wake afer sleep onset were also found to be useful. However, time to sleep onset obtained by actigraphy had lower consistency, and, in general, correlations were found to be reduced in severely disturbed sleep. Good correlation between actigraphy and PSG were also obtained in studies involving infants and children. In subjects with severe sleep apnea and those on antidepressants, the correlation was lower compared to PSG.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: Various factors like the model of the actigraph, the population under study, the device settings, and the algorithm employed can infuence the total sleep duration obtained using actigraphy. Also, actigraphy may not correlate well with PSG at each minute, especially in cases of disturbed sleep. Variation has also been noted between different devices; thus, the investigator has to be cautious when comparing results from studies using diferent devices. Reliability studies are required for each model of actigraph and for the specifc population group being studied.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: APPLICATIONS

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: Actigraphy is a reliable tool in the assessment of sleep in normal populations. However, it may not be

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: reliable in many sleep disorders. AASM has given conditional recommendations for the use of actigraphy in the assessment of following conditions:

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ● Insomnia disorder (in adult patients to esti­

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: mate sleep parameters and in pediatric patients for assessment)

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ● Circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder (in adults and pediatric patients)

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ● To estimate total sleep time (TST) integrated with home sleep apnea test devices, in the evaluation of patients suspected to have sleep disordered breathing

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ● Monitoring total duration of sleep before a Multiple Sleep Latency Test in adult and pediatric patients in whom a central disorder of hypersomnolence is suspected—to ensure adequate sleep prior to testing

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ● Insufcient sleep syndrome-to estimate TST

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: In addition, a strong recommendation to not use actigraphy as a monitoring device for movements in the diagnosis of periodic limb movement disorder has been given.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: Actigraphy is also useful for studying the efects of treatment due to its ability to identify changes in sleep patterns over time. In addition, it can be used

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: Limitations 125

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: during follow-up assessments during the course of treatment and also to screen patients for sleep problems.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: Te additional parameters recorded by the actigraph can be useful in specifc conditions. Ambient light measurements comprising the amount and duration of light exposure are useful in studying advanced and delayed sleep-wake phase disorders. Tis can also aid in the development of a treatment plan. Some actigraphs have a built-in microphone to detect snoring, and some can measure skin temperature, which is useful in the study of circadian rhythm. Actigraphy with extended EEG, EMG, and EOG capability, such that objective scoring of stages is possible, is also available for commercial use. Actigraphy is also available with extended ECG recording capability.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: Actigraphy can be used in research and has been used in many cohort studies of the relation between sleep and various health parameters. Te relatively low cost, better subject compliance, and ease of use make actigraphy a useful tool in large population studies. Study areas have included the relationship of sleep with outcomes such as impaired cognition, propensity for falls, reduced exercise performance, risk of obesity, and serum cholesterol levels. One such study done in an elite archer using actigraphy with EEG module is placed in suggested reading for those interested.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: APPLICATIONS

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: Various commercially available devices are marketed as having the capability to assess sleep. Tese include smartphone applications that make use of the accelerometer in the device and smartwatches such as Fitbit and Apple watch worn on the wrist. Some smartwatches use accelerometers similar to the ones used in actigraphy. In addition, they are more widely available, cheaper, and the results are easy to interpret. While smartphones may not accurately depict sleep, few smartwatches have given results comparable to actigraphy. Some of these devices may be a good start for monitoring sleep in otherwise healthy people, but there is a need to check the validation of the device before use. For research, most of these devices don’t provide access to the raw data for more in-depth analysis.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: Sleep applications can draw from multiple modalities that include both built-in and external sensors and questionnaires. Hence, they can provide more detailed analysis, including sleep stages. However, most of such applications are not scientifcally validated and give results in formats that are difcult to convert to standard sleep parameters. Some studies have shown that they have comparable accuracy to actigraphy in sleep-wake discrimination. In addition, there are apps specifcally designed to detect snoring/OSA, which have specifc algorithms.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: Such devices and applications would require more validation studies before they can be used for the clinical assessment of sleep.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ADVANTAGES

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: While actigraphy cannot be a substitute for PSG, it has many advantages, thus making it a useful tool in a sleep medicine physician’s arsenal. Tey include:

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ● Convenient and low patient burden, less inva­

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: sive than PSG.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ● Relatively low cost.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ● Data that are continuous and objective in con­

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: trast to a sleep diary, which gives discrete and subjective data.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ● Elimination of laboratory efects as the subjects can sleep in their own homes.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ● Longitudinal assessment capability as the device can be worn 24 hours/day for extended durations.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ● Ability to be used to assess treatment response and in follow-up.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ● More reliable estimates of sleep as data are col­

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: lected over multiple nights.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ● In pediatric populations, reduction of the care­

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: giver’s burden and minimization of issues of compliance to sleep logs by the child/caregiver, who can ofen be unreliable.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: LIMITATIONS

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ● Although cheaper than PSG, actigraphy is still costlier when compared to sleep diaries or sleep questionnaires.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ● Actigraphy is currently not reliable enough to be recommended as a stand-alone method for the diagnosis of a sleep disorder.

text: ● While actigraphy in its usual form can distin­

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: polysomnography and should be used where recommended. However, relying on it totally where an overnight polysomnography is indicated might mislead the physician. Actigraphy devices with built-in features may be an option to explore. Actigraphy remains an important tool in outlying areas where overnight polysomnography is not available.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: guish between wake and sleep, it has not been validated for measuring sleep stages.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ● Validity is limited in the estimation of sleep onset latency and daytime sleeping.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ● Since it can incorrectly classify a subject who is awake but lying motionless as asleep, actigraphy can overestimate TST and thus underestimate the sleep disturbance. Tis is especially important in hospitalized and bed-bound individuals as they may not have much activity while awake.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ● Although no major adverse efects are associ­

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report
text: ated with the use of actigraphy, some patients may develop a minor skin irritation, and few may have difculty sleeping because of wearing the actigraphy watch.

chapter: 18 Actigraphy: Indications, Procedural Do’s and Don’ts, Sample Report

chapter: 19 Home Sleep Apnea Testing
text: In 2007, the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality published a landmark article reassessing the state of the art in our understanding of homebased diagnostics for sleep apnea. Tis analysis was an evidence-based prelude to the 2007 Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) reexamination of the evidence for home sleep apnea testing, which led to its decision in 2008 to allow home sleep apnea testing results to be used for the provision of CPAP therapy for sleep apnea.

chapter: 19 Home Sleep Apnea Testing
text: With regard to home sleep apnea testing (HSAT), when combined with clinical history, for many forms of home sleep apnea technology currently in existence, there was no conclusive evidence that it was substantially better or substantially worse than traditional PSG for making a diagnosis of OSA. Teir decision has allowed for type 3, type 2, and type 1 monitors to be more or less equivalent for allowing a diagnosis of sleep apnea in order to provide CPAP therapy. Level 4 monitors were excluded from this approval. However, the fnal national coverage determination (NCD) developed a category called level 4 with three channels that are covered by CMS.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: Polysomnography is a recording of multiple physiological variables to study the physiological changes that occur in sleep and to correlate them to the various stages of sleep. Essentially the digital polysomnography records the various phases of sleep-wake (wake, REM, and NREM sleep); picks up artifacts; analyzes the ECG for rate, rhythm, heart rate variability (if possible), pulse saturations; analyzes respiratory movements and oronasal airfow to check for apnea, types of apnea (obstructive or central, hypopnea, respiratoryevent-related arousal [RERA], and noninvasive blood pressure using pulse transit time and ECG

text: HISTORY

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: In the early twentieth century, emerging evidence appeared regarding the role of the EEG in psychology and psychiatry, and recordings of these signals were conducted for research. In 1928, Hans Berger, a German psychiatrist, recorded electrical activity of the human brain. He called these recordings ‘electroencephalograms,’ known today as EEG.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: WHAT IS POLYSOMNOGRAPHY?

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: It was also found that EEG recordings showed a marked diference in the sleep and wake states. Characterization of human sleep occurred in 1937, when Davis et al. at Harvard University studied sleep brain wave patterns and characterized human sleep. High-amplitude low-frequency slow waves and spindles characterized human sleep, and lowamplitude high-frequency beta waves and alpha rhythm were used for characterization of wakefulness. Te unitary concept of sleep prevailed until Eugene Aserinsky, a graduate student of Kleitman in 1952, was assigned the job to observe eye movements in infants and later also in adults while asleep.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: Following this, a method of electrooculography (EOG) for continuously measuring eye movements was devised. Several bursts of potential changes on EOG were recorded during sleep, and they were quite diferent from the slow movements at sleep onset. Te seminal paper in 1953 by Aserinsky and Kleitman was a breakthrough in sleep research as the duality of sleep—REM and non-REM or NREM came into being. Wholenight recordings were still not done in order to conserve paper as there was a paucity of funds, but in 1959, motivated by Aserinsky’s results, Dement and Kleitman recorded 126 full-night recordings with 33 subjects and, with the help of EEG patterns, scored the paper recordings in their entirety. When the scoring was complete, they correlated the patterns and found that these patterns occurred repeatedly at an interval of approximately 90–110 minutes while the subject was asleep. A cyclical nature was determined, and NREM and REM percentages of the total sleep time were also found. Te suppression of muscle potentials during REM sleep in cats was studied by Michel Jouvet. In the 1960s, Hodes and Dement worked on the H refex in humans and found the complete suppression of H refex during REM sleep, and the importance of electromyography during sleep recording was realized.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: Tus, for delineating the diferent stages of sleep and distinguishing them from wake, EEG, EOG, and EMG recordings are essential.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: In 1968, Rechtschafen and Kales propounded sleep staging criteria using EEG, EOG, and EMG. Jerome Holland at Stanford University coined the term “polysomnography” in 1974 and added cardiac and respiratory sensors to the EEG, EOG, and EMG.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: Polysomnography is the recording of various biological signals during sleep. Tese signals provide diferent information regarding the physiological variables. Tis information helps in scoring sleep or in monitoring physiology during sleep: for example, heart rate information from ECG; airfow trace from an oronasal thermistor; respiratory efort from thoracic and abdominal efort belts, etc. In other words, polysomnography is a multichannel record designed to document a variety of physiological activities during sleep.

text: MONTAGE AND SENSORS

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: A standard PSG montage requires an EEG, EMG, ECG, oronasal thermistor, nasal cannula, limb leads, pulse oximeter, respiratory efort belts, body position sensor, and snoring sensor. A PAP device fow may be required where CPAP would be used during the study for titrations. Recommended flter settings and sampling rates for the proper acquisition of the data from various sensors are required. Most of the digital acquisition machines follow AASM guidelines, and compliance should be ensured in the montage before starting the study. Te montage is completed with the location of EEG channels and marking the location of ground and reference electrodes.

3. Cases of sleep disorders on treatment, not responding to therapy or showing emergence of new symptoms; or suspicion of development of any other coexisting disorder. PSG is indicated in:

Follow-up PSG in adults is indicated when, despite PAP therapy, symptoms start to recur, and response to PAP needs to be assessed; weight gain or loss afer PAP therapy starts; recent change in blood pressure, arrythmias at night, TIA/stroke despite being on PAP (required to reassess the sleep-related hypoxemia). 4. Similarly, when NREM parasomnias, epilepsy, nocturnal enuresis is present, screening for OSA or PLMD are required, PSG is indicated. 5. chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: PSG is not indicated for establishing a diagnosis of insomnia, sleep deprivation, shif work disorder, DSWPD, ASWPD, jet lag syndrome alone. It is not recommended for sleep-related bruxism in children. However, if these disorders are suspected with another disorder or if child does not respond with the recommended therapy, PSG is indicated to ascertain the diagnosis.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: EEG, EOG, and EMG Channels

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: Te EEG, EOG, and EMG are recorded afer placing electrodes on the scalp and skin surfaces. Te site is cleaned and properly prepared with skin preparation gel to ensure a good contact such that the electrical impedance is kept at 5000 Ω or less. Scalp electrodes are afxed with electrode conductive paste. Electrode application to identify location is as per the EEG Society’s international 10–20 system. A montage using only F3, F4, O1, O2, C3, and C4 positions is used as a standard EEG montage for PSG and referenced to the contralateral mastoid. F3, O1, and C3 are placed as a backup in case the contralateral corresponding side is moved or removed from the scalp during sleep.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: EOG channels, one on each side at the outer canthi, are placed, the right EOG electrode 1 cm above and the lef electrode 1 cm below the outer canthus. Tis placement helps to identify both horizontal and vertical movements of the eye.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: EMG Channels

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: A pair of electrodes are placed at the submentalis muscle for recording EMG. One electrode is placed at the midline, 1 cm above the mandible’s inferior edge, and is referenced to another one placed 2 cm below and 2 cm to the right (or lef) from this reference electrode. Practically at night, if both right and lef electrodes are applied, then one of them intends to act as backup in case one of them loses contact with the skin surface.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: BIOCALIBRATION

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: Before starting the study, biocalibration using common instructions is done: for example, types of eye movements (moving up/down; right/lef; fast blinks, reading type), grinding teeth, moving legs, taking a deep breath and stopping it, breathing slowly and then rapidly to check fow, pressure and the respiratory efort. Te individual is asked to count slowly, and the snoring sensor trace checked. Closing the eyes shows alpha waves at the occipital area in alpha generators and helps identify the alpha block once the individual now opens the eyes. Once the alpha waves are seen, the attenuation of these waves by 50% in an epoch can be kept as a criterion for N1, along with slowly rolling eye movements and the vertex wave. Tis is important not only to check that the sensors are connected, and acquisition is fne but also to check back on some recording with these markings like eye movements for the type of sleep, etc.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: Artifact Detection

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: Artifacts are signals that are extraneous in nature and afect the analysis. A signal that interferes with the analysis of another is also considered an

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: artifact: for example, if an ECG trace is recorded in the EEG trace, ECG is the artifact in the EEG recording. Artifacts may originate either from the patient, e.g., from sweat, an ECG trace in the EEG signal, eye movements trace in the EEG. Tey may be due to the equipment: e.g., a broken or faulty electrode, improper connection of the lead to the headbox; a sensor not connected at all, etc. Or they may be due to the external factors, such as 50/60 Hz impedance. Te common types of artifacts seen during the study are sweat artifacts, ECG trace seen in EEG/EOG trace, movement artifacts, snore artifacts, incorrect flter or gain settings, 60/50 Hz impedance or high impedance, or artifacts emerging because of an electrode popping of the subject.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: Recognizing these artifacts is important, and troubleshooting is extremely vital for a clean polysomnography record. At the start of the study, in case an artifact is seen, one can check the montage and its setting, recalibrate the amplifer, and, if still not corrected, try to identify the type of artifact. ECG artifacts in the EEG trace can be simply corrected at the start of the study. In case it is missed, some machines have an option of ECG correction which is done by eliminating the ECG signal from the trace where the artifact is visible. Ideally it should be checked initially and amended at the start of the study by changing the location of the electrode.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: At the start of the study, if the tracing appears artifact free, and then, during the study, artifacts appear, adequate trouble shooting is required. Sweat artifacts appear as slow waves and may mimic delta waves. Te appearance of these in a few EEG channels and the lack of disappearance even when the stage appears to have changed from N3 to N1/N2/REM/wake in other channels should raise an alarm and help identify the sweat artifact.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: Some golden rules for correction of artifacts once identifed are as follows:

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: ● If the artifact appears in a channel to which backup is already available, such as the chin EMG, alternate EEG channel, etc., then let the patient sleep and do not try to fx the problem during the study.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: ● If the artifact is appearing in multiple EEG electrodes, look for a common source: the contralateral mastoid for all common electrodes on one side; the ground electrode if all EEG electrodes are involved, etc. Also look carefully

text: ● If afer checking all the wires, electrodes, con­

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: Scoring Rules for Staging Sleep

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: Te night record is scored epoch-wise. For sleep staging, a standard 30 second epoch is taken, and each epoch scored as per the recommended criteria of the American Association of Sleep Medicine (AASM). Broad guidelines of scoring the wake and various stages of sleep are discussed next.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: ● Wake: Beta waves or low-amplitude mixedfrequency EEG; reading eye movements, eye blinks, and irregular conjugate eye movements are seen. Alpha waves appear especially at the occipital region when eyes are closed but the individual is awake.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: ● NREM: Tis type of sleep has four stages: I, II, III and IV. Rechtschafen and Kales criteria are used for all stages, but as per the AASM guideline, stages III and IV are combined as N3 during the scoring and staging of sleep. Te identifying features of each are as follows:

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: ● N1: Individuals who generate alpha waves on EEG when eyes closed but are awake show more than 50% attenuation of alpha in an epoch, and the EEG now shows low amplitude mixed frequency during N1 sleep. Tis is accompanied by slow rolling movements in EOG, and there may be a slight reduction in EMG tone as compared to wake. Vertex wave may be seen, which is sharp and of less than 0.5 second duration.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: ● N2: N2 sleep is characterized by one or more K-complexes and one and more trains of sleep spindles that are not associated with arousal. EEG remains low amplitude mixed frequency, but

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: intermittently one sees K-complex and spindles. K-complex is a typical sharp negative, followed by a large positive wave. Te entire duration of K-complex is more than 0.5 second and is seen maximally at the frontal location. Spindles are 12–14 Hz waves maximally seen at a central location, and duration is more than 0.5 second.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: ● An individual in N2 can proceed to N3, may have an arousal or body movements, and slip to stage N1 or wake. Te subject may also show REM sleep afer N2.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: ● N3: Tis stage is called the slow wave sleep stage. Tis comprises both stage III and stage IV. N3 is scored when an epoch shows more than 20% of the epoch with delta waves. Delta waves characteristically are 0.5–4 Hz maximally seen at the central region, and the amplitude of these waves is more than 75 µV.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: ● R: REM sleep is scored when the EEG shows low amplitude high frequency. Tere is minimal EMG tone seen in the chin EMG as compared to wake and NREM. Tere are rapid, irregular, sharply peaked conjugate eye movements. Due to the appearance of the EEG being like wake, it is also called paradoxical sleep.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: Te details on scoring various stages, along with transition from one stage to another, follow AASM guidelines.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: Scoring Events

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: What events should one look for in the polysomnography record, and how should one score them?

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: While scrolling through the polysomnography epochs, one should look for unusual occurrences like a change in EMG tone, movements, artifacts, arousals, arrhythmias, abnormal behavior, abnormal breathing patterns, etc. For beginners, it is advisable to do the scoring of events afer the scoring for staging sleep is done. Some common events are mentioned in brief here. Recent AASM guidelines should be checked for scoring these events in detail.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: When Is It an Arousal?

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: Arousal is a sudden shif in EEG frequency of more than 16 Hz. First, it should be confrmed that they

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: Scoring and Reporting the Study 139

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: are not spindles. Tis shif in frequency should be afer at least 10 seconds of stable sleep to be called an arousal and should last for at least 3 seconds. If marked during REM, it should have an increase in EMG tone for at least a second. Te arousal index is calculated by multiplying 60 with the number of arousals during the record and dividing it by total sleep time (TST).

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: Whenever an arousal is noted, which is marked automatically by digital polysomnography sofware, we should ascertain and confrm its presence and then try to fnd out a cause, if any. For example, is it related to desaturation due to a respiratory problem, apnea, hypopnea, arrhythmia, periodic limb movement, body movements, or is it spontaneous, i.e., without any evident cause?

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: When Is It a Periodic Limb

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: Movement?

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: A periodic limb movement is scored when a limb movement is not within 0.5 second (neither preceding nor following the movement) of an apnea, hypopnea, or respiratory-event-related arousal or sleep disordered breathing. An increase of a minimum 8 µV from the baseline EMG tone marks the start of period and should last at least 0.5 second to 10 seconds until the time when the EMG does not exceed 2 µV above resting. A minimum number of 4 such limb movements with a minimum period of 5 second and maximum until 90 seconds is required to score it as a limb movement. If the leg movements on both limbs are separated by less than 5 seconds, then they are considered a single event.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: What Should Be Reported from

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: an ECG Trace?

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: ECG recording from lead II can be used for screening various events. If the sampling rate is higher than 256 Hz, it is even better. As per current guidelines, 500 Hz is desired for this reason as it helps discern the events of higher frequencies better. Heart rate and its alterations can be reported for the night using the ECG trace. Sinus bradycardia less than 40 bpm, sinus tachycardia more than 90 bpm, asystole more than 3 seconds, with heart rate more than 100 bpm if the QRS duration is less than 120 ms, is scored as narrow complex tachycardia. It is scored as wide complex tachycardia if the QRS

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: duration is more than 120 ms for a consecutive 3 beats. Any evidence of atrial fbrillation, any other arrhythmia should be reported. Any sign of ischemia or infarction should be reported. At times these events may corroborate the technician notes during the night where it is recorded by the technician that the patient was uncomfortable, sweating, woke up with complaints of feeling not well, felt sufocated, needed to get a breath of fresh air and so woke up, and many other related complaints, and hence events should be also referred to the technician notes.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: Te ECG trace can be used along with pulse plethysmography trace to measure pulse transit time (PTT). PTT can be used to measure blood pressure indirectly.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: Traces from the nasal cannula and oronasal cannula monitor pressure and are best to pick up hypopnea, while the oronasal thermistor indicates apnea by measuring the fow. Hypopnea is a more than 30% drop in peak signal as compared to pre-event baseline in the cannula trace. Duration should be more than 10 seconds. Tis reduced excursion may be associated with an arousal. Apnea is a sudden cessation of breath for more than 10 seconds as seen on the thermistor trace.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: EMG trace at the chin can be used for bruxism, and limb leads may give a clue for REM behavior disorder. Arousal may lead to increased EMG tone in either of the traces.

chapter: 20 Polysomnography I: Detail with Indications, Hookup Procedure, Do’s and Don’ts
text: A good acquisition of data and grasp of the knowledge of the changes during sleep and of scoring sleep are the most important requirements for the study. A trained technician and a relatively noise-free room with a comfortable bed and bedding makes this type of study the gold standard. Tough it is cost-intensive due to infrastructural, personnel, and equipment requirements, but, in complicated cases, it can clinch the diagnosis for better management and clinical outcomes.

text: REVIEW OF SLEEP HYGIENE

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Sleep hygiene is a practice of multiple behavior changes that lead to better-quality sleep. Good-quality sleep hygiene is important before scheduling a sleep study or for treating any sleep disorder. Sleep hygiene is one of the most important interventions that works on the basic physiologic principles and resets the sleep parameters to its natural form. Patient use of cafeine, and diferent forms should be discussed, and education provided. Signifcant marijuana smoking as well as other nicotine products should not be used close to bedtime. Routine exercise has signifcant value in regulating sleep. Maintenance of a comfortable bed and pillow, bedroom temperature and lighting, as well as a sleep-conducive ambience in the bedroom are important in accomplishing

text: restorative sleep. Te patient’s inability to sleep sometimes stems from other coexistent insomnia or mostly generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) or situational anxiety. Multiple resources are available for intervention both with pharmaceutical and nonpharmaceutical approaches. Both medical and mental conditions tend to afect sleep negatively. Te control of the comorbid conditions is important especially when it relates to chronic pain, gastrointestinal disturbance, and similar uncomfortable conditions. Review of patient medications, including prescription and over the counter, as well as herbal products, is important as nearly all the medications afect sleep negatively or positively. Many medications suppress REM sleep or non-REM sleep. Withdrawal from this medication can bring about a rebound of the suppressed sleep stage.

text: STUDY REPORT

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Afer the overnight polysomnography, multiple parameters are recorded, and data are collected. As previously mentioned, these parameters record an electroencephalogram, electrooculogram, electromyogram, and electrocardiogram, as well as monitoring the airfow, chest movement abdominal movement, leg movements, and snoring oxygen saturation. Te data are organized into diferent sections for reporting purposes. Te sections include the patient identifcation and the demographic data, technical details regarding the process that was used in the setting of the sleep study with the methodology and review of monitored parameters. A summary of the patient’s complaint, historical fndings, and physical examination fndings are recorded in the following section. Tis information is critical and applies the results of the sleep study to the patient’s chief complaint, as well as the efect of the patient’s comorbid conditions and medications on the sleep architecture as recorded. Te next section records the cardiac activity and fndings during sleep and respiratory events including apneas, hypopneas, respiratory-efort-related arousals, oxygen desaturation, and apnea hypopnea index.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Another section of the report is dedicated to the movement-related sleep disorders and records the periodic limb movements of sleep. Afer review of the fndings as mentioned previously, an interpretive statement is made by the physician who reviewed the raw data and the compilation of fndings in the sleep study report.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: TERMINOLOGY REVIEW

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Te section that reports sleep architecture includes total recording time (TRT), time in bed (TIB), and total sleep time (TST).

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: TRT is the time that represents how long the recording equipment was activated while the patient was in bed.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: TIB is important in establishing how long the subject was indeed trying to fall asleep. If the patient does not spend time in bed, then the total sleep time is going to be low and will cause symptoms consistent with insufficient sleep syndrome.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Sleep latency is the time from lights out to sleep onset. Te upper end of sleep latency is considered to be 30 minutes. Long sleep latency is seen in patients with insomnia and other similar disorders. On the other hand, short sleep latency can be seen in patients who have been sleep deprived or who have taken certain medications with hypnotic efects. Special attention must be paid to the patient’s habitual sleep time and wake time to adjust the lights out and lights on times during sleep study.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: TST is the total sleep time that is scored from sleep onset to fnal awakening. Te durations of awakenings in between are deducted from total sleep time. Total sleep time certainly provides signifcant information regarding the amount of sleep a patient is able to get.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: ● Short total sleep time can be seen in patients with insomnia, comorbid medical conditions, chronic pain, and sometimes medications or substance use.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: ● Long total sleep time can be seen in patients who are recovering from sleep deprivation or who have medical conditions afecting sleep. Medications and substance use can also increase total sleep time.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Sleep efciency is the percentage of total time in bed compared to actual sleep recorded. Sleep efciency is a good overall refection of the quality of sleep.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: ● Low sleep efciency can result from multiple factors that include long sleep latency and early morning awakenings with long sleep onset time.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: ● High sleep efciency is associated with recov­

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: ery sleep and the efect of the medications.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Wake afer sleep onset (WASO) refers to the wakeful time during the sleep, between the sleep onset and sleep ofset. Tis time is calculated by adding all the episodes of awakening during the night. WASO refects sleep fragmentation and indicates nonrestorative sleep.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Wake time afer sleep onset (WASO) refects the early morning awakening generally seen in patients with depression. Tis can also be seen naturally in older age in the elderly with no difculty in falling asleep but they wake up early afer a short sleep.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Review of Respiratory Events 143

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: REM latency is the time from sleep onset to the frst episode of the REM sleep. It is afected by multiple factors, including the efect of the medications or withdrawal.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: RAPID EYE MOVEMENT (REM)

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: SLEEP

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: ● Short REM latency can be seen in withdrawal from TCA antidepressant medications, MAO inhibitors, barbiturates, alcohol, and amphetamines. Many medical conditions like narcolepsy, sleep apnea, and depression also contribute to short REM latency.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: ● Long REM latency occurs when REMsuppressing medications are used; for example, TCA, intermittent amphetamine, alcohol, and barbiturates are some representative drugs.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: SLEEP STAGES

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Tis section of the polysomnography reports the percentage of area sleep stages. In general, stage N1 is approximately 5% of the total sleep time, stage N2 is 50%, stage N3 is 20%, and stage REM is 25% of the total sleep time.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Non-rapid Eye Movement (Non-REM)

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Sleep

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Stage N1 sleep transitions from wakefulness to sleep and is a state of drowsiness. An increased quantity and percentage of N1 sleep refect sleep fragmentation. It can be caused by the frequent arousals throughout the night. Clinical examples include periodic limb movements of sleep and obstructive sleep apnea.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Stage N2 sleep is the most prevalent sleep stage. It takes approximately 50% of the total sleep time. Increased N2 sleep is seen with age and medication efect. Decreased N2 sleep is a result of sleep fragmentation, increasing other stages of sleep like REM or stage N3. N2 sleep is also decreased in obstructive sleep apnea patients.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Stage N3 sleep is known by diferent names, including delta sleep or slow wave sleep. A high amount of N3 sleep is seen in the frst half of the night. Increased N3 sleep is noted in rebound sleep afer sleep deprivation or afer the initiation of positive airway pressure therapy in sleep disordered breathing patients. Decreased N3 sleep is seen with efective medications, especially benzodiazepines, barbiturates, and TCAs.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: REM sleep constitutes approximately 25% of the total sleep time. REM sleep generally dominates the second half of the night. REM sleep alternates with non-REM sleep in cycles of 80–110 minutes. A total of 4–5 cycles can be completed during 1 night of sleep. As the night progresses, the length of the REM sleep continues to gradually increase with the longest REM in the early morning hours.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: An increase in REM sleep was noted in recovery sleep afer sleep deprivation and withdrawal from REM-suppressing medications.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: A decrease in REM sleep occurs with the efect of medications like barbiturates, TCAs, MAO inhibitors, and anticholinergic medications and afer meals.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: REVIEW OF RESPIRATORY EVENTS

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Respiratory events are reported in a separate section. Tis is one of the most important sections of the report as the diagnosis of sleep disordered breathing is based on the fndings of the recorded events calculated per hour of sleep. Te following fve events are reported:

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Obstructive apnea: Cessation of airfow from the nose and mouth lasting 10 seconds or longer that may or may not have accompanying SA02 desaturation Central apnea: Cessation of airfow from the nose and mouth and absence of diaphragmatic and abdominal eforts lasting 10 seconds or longer; may or may not have accompanying SA02 desaturation Mixed apnea: Cessation of airfow from the nose and mouth, beginning with the absence of diaphragmatic and abdominal eforts lasting 10 seconds or longer; may or may not have accompanying SA02 desaturation Hypopnea: A decrease in airfow from the nose and mouth and a decrease in amplitude of diaphragmatic and abdominal eforts lasting 10 seconds or longer, followed by an arousal that must be associated with 02 desaturation equal to or greater than 3% Respiratory-efort-related arousal (RERA):

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Periodic limb movements index in wake and sleep are:

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: The apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) is the sum of total apneas and hypopneas noted over the total sleep time. The apnea hypopnea index is arguably the most important parameter documented in the sleep study report. The index allows the provider to assess the risk of potential complications related to sleep disordered breathing (obstructive sleep apnea). Treatment decisions are based on the apnea-hypopnea index, which serves as a measure of the efficacy of the applied treatment.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Te apnea hypopnea index is:

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: ● Normal if it is less than 5.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: ● Mild from 5 to 14 events per hour.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: ● Severe over 30 events per hour.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Te respiratory distress index (RDI) is the sum of total apneas, hypopneas, and respiratoryefort-related arousals.

text: REVIEW OF PERIODIC LIMB

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: MOVEMENTS

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Periodic limb movements are repetitive movements that frequently involve fexion of the toes, ankle, knee, and hip. Due to these movements, some patients report difculty falling asleep or sleep maintenance insomnia. Tese movements can impact daytime functioning and can cause fatigue and daytime sleepiness.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Tey are generally divided into:

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: ● Limb movements in sleep (PLMS) frequently noted when the limb activity is monitored by EMG during sleep.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: ● Periodic limb movement disorder (PLMD) is documented when the periodic limb movement of sleep is associated with daytime or nighttime symptoms.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: If PLMs are found to be part of another sleep disorder like restless leg syndrome (RLS), then the underlying primary sleep disorder should be treated.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Te movements occur during REM (loss of atonia).

text: AROUSAL EVENTS

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Te total number of arousals and awakenings is reported as a frequency per hour of sleep and is referred to as an index. Even with a mild arousal index, obviously sleep is interrupted and will cause daytime symptoms of tiredness and fatigue.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Video recordings are important in capturing the details of patient behavior, activity, and abnormal movements; video complements the waveform recordings and makes the interpretations more accurate. Video and audio features are important both in adults and in pediatric sleep studies. Video recording truly enhances the quality of the sleep study and allows identifcation of the disorders that may not be obvious from the waveform analysis:

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: A hypnogram is a composite graphic display of the overnight sleep-wake stages, respiratory events, and other recorded parameters in the polysomnogram. Te hypnogram gives a bird’s-eye view on a single page, where events can be correlated to the activity occurring at the same time in diferent channels. Sleep structure can be easily characterized by review of the hypnogram:

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: PRACTICE IMPLICATIONS

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Te report of the sleep study is an excellent document not only that provides information regarding the confrmation of the clinical diagnosis as

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: it relates to the patient’s chief complaint but that has comprehensive details regarding the diferent stages of sleep on the timeline of 6–8 hours of total sleep time. Tese parameters and observations help in clinical decision making and recommendations regarding better-quality sleep. Each parameter derived from the collected data has a signifcant impact on the general information and lifestyle changes. A focused recommendation can be made regarding changes to be made in sleep time, exercise, and substance use. It also shows the impact of diferent medical and psychiatric conditions as well as the medication efect on the overall quality of the sleep. Appropriate adjustments can be made in the management of these disorders or medications.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: If the sleep study includes CPAP titration, then further recommendations can be made regarding the pressure to be used and the type of the mask interface, humidity settings, as well as the ramp function settings.

chapter: 21 Polysomnography II: Sample Reports with Explanation of Various Terminologies
text: Review of the sleep study further emphasizes patient follow-up on a regular basis in order to troubleshoot any improvement-related problems and to assess the efcacy of the CPAP therapy. Sometimes underlying disorders surface once the obstructive sleep apnea is treated. Tese visits provide an opportunity to discover other disorders that were not evident due to the presence of sleep disordered breathing.

text: INTRODUCTION

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: Te nonpharmacological approach to a sleep problem may be used to avoid development of a sleep disorder in cases where the sleep problem is still a symptom and not a disorder. It can be used as an adjunct in the overall management of sleep disorders.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: Tough the nonpharmacological approach is ofen referred to for insomnia, it may also be applied to lifestyle modifcations for weight loss, especially for obstructive sleep apnea, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), and for disorders other than insomnia, e.g., depression, anxiety etc. Positive airway pressure and oral appliance therapy for the management of obstructive sleep apnea are discussed in detail in Chapters 25 and 26. Similarly, a behavioral approach is found to be efective for children with bed wetting problems and night waking, but that is beyond the scope of this chapter.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: Tis chapter emphasizes on the nonpharmacological approach in adults for chronic insomnia, which includes principles of sleep hygiene, CBT for

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: Sleep Hygiene 150 Complementary and Alternate

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: COGNITIVE, PSYCHOLOGICAL,

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: AND BEHAVIORAL TREATMENT

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: As per AASM guidelines, multicomponent CBTI is strongly recommended for treatment of chronic insomnia patients. It usually takes 4–8 sessions, and the efect starts to appear gradually and steadily.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: CBT suitability to the patient should be judged by both the referring primary care physician and the therapist. CBTI includes sleep restriction, stimulus control therapy, relaxation-based interventions, cognitive strategies, and sleep hygiene education. For insomnia, it is aimed at the pathophysiology of insomnia explained by Spielman’s 3P model: precipitating, predisposing, and perpetuating factors. Tese factors can be specifcally identifed in the patient with regular interviews and noted. Predispositions added with perpetuating

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: 150 Sleep Hygiene and Nonpharmacological Interventions

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: factors precipitate conditions to prolong the insomnia. Once the factors are clear, a directed approach toward developing strategies to mitigate them can be developed.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: STIMULUS CONTROL

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: Behavioral therapy is comprised of sleep hygiene, sleep restriction, stimulus control, and relaxation training. Cognitive strategy aims at restructuring cognitive beliefs that hamper sleep. Tis multicomponent therapy using cognitive and behavioral therapy comprises CBTI.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: Te idea of CBTI is not to change personality traits but insight-oriented psychotherapy with respect to the predisposing and perpetuating factors. CBTI is based on the premise of maladaptive cognitions that, according to Beck’s theory, include general beliefs about the world, the self, and the future, giving rise to specifc and automatic thoughts in particular situations that, when targeted with therapeutic strategies, lead to changes in emotional distress and behaviors. Patients motivated to work on their maladaptive beliefs perform better. Specifc problem areas, once identifed, help the therapist to formulate specifc targeted goals for therapy. Te therapy is gradual and slow to show improvement, and hence observing patience on the part of the patient and therapist is the key to successful outcomes.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: Multicomponent CBTI is comprised of sleep hygiene, sleep education, sleep restriction, stimulus control, and relaxation therapy.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: SLEEP RESTRICTION

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: In this component of multicomponent CBTI, the individual is instructed to restrict the time in bed. Tis is done to improve sleep efciency, which is the time slept divided by the time in bed as a percentage. If the sleep efciency is lesser than 85%, sleep restriction can reduce the time in bed, hence increasing the sleep efciency percentage. Te amount of time in bed should not be reduced to less than 6 hours in any case. Such sleep restriction can cause sleep deprivation and, in some patients, may cause daytime fatigue, sleepiness during daytime, irritability, and attention problems due to lack of sleep. Hence the clinician should avoid further sleep restriction in patients complaining of the side efects just mentioned due to sleep deprivation efects. It is contraindicated in heavy-duty machine operators, patients with history of mania or hypomania, and cases predisposed to or sufering from seizure disorders.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: Te bed or bedroom is associated with sleep or sexual activity. Te individual is asked to follow this strictly such that the stimulus of bed or being in the bedroom becomes associated with sleeping. If the patient is not able to sleep for 15–20 minutes afer lying in bed to sleep, the individual is advised to get out of bed and return when sleepy. A fxed wake-up time is advised to be followed.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: RELAXATION THERAPY

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: Relaxation therapy is an important component of CBTI. It aims to reduce sleep onset or wake afer sleep onset. Progressive muscular relaxation is frequently used. Appropriate training for the individual should be imparted by the therapist to instill confdence in the patient and to ensure compliance.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: SLEEP HYGIENE

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: Sleep hygiene alone as a single component is not recommended by the AASM for treatment of chronic insomnia in adults. Sleep hygiene principles are habits that improve sleep. Tey can be explained in two ways. First is a didactic method, in which all the principles are explained to the individual. Second, the points that need to be dealt with due to the individual’s complaining of the inability to sleep or due to a problem are addressed afer a brief interview analyzing the individual’s habits. Te principles of sleep hygiene primarily involve the habit of making a consistent routine with a set bedtime and wake time for both weekdays and weekends. It includes indulging in relaxing activities and avoiding stimulants before sleep. Stimulants like smoking before bedtime are best avoided. Alcohol is ofen misused to help in falling asleep. Tough the patient goes of to sleep afer becoming drunk, the efect of alcohol is actually deleterious to sleep. It afects the maintenance of sleep and causes frequent awakenings and an unrefreshed sleep. It is recommended to avoid alcohol at bedtime. In the case of increased presleep arousal, reserve cafeine for the morning hours. A relaxed schedule at bedtime, and the avoidance of bright light exposure before sleep helps.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: Tough these are general tips for improving sleep in a healthy population, in sleep disorders it

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: Sleep Hygiene 151

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: becomes an important part of the nonpharmacological approach to the patient management strategy. Some points for patients:

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: ● Keep a consistent bedtime and wakeup time. Te total time in bed should be at least 7–8 hours; adequate opportunity to sleep should be provided by the patient for sleep. Having a consistent bedtime and wakeup time both on weekdays and weekends is crucial to avoid sleep deprivation. Unless the patient needs to entrain to a new timing, which should be planned as per the disorder under consultation, this consistent schedule should be followed.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: ● Avoid studying in bed and only use bed for sleep and sex.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: ● Unwind before sleep time. Indulge in relaxing activities and avoid stimulants before bedtime. Alcohol consumption before bedtime is known to deteriorate sleep quality. Afer alcohol, the patient may sleep easily and so is even used to go to sleep in cases of sleep onset insomnia, but alcohol makes the patient keep on waking up during the night and impairs the sleep quality. Smoking before sleep time should be best avoided due to the stimulant action on the body. Cafeine should be restricted from the afernoon onwards, if one is sensitive and sleep onset is afected. Preferably no cafeine within 4–5 hours of bedtime is a good habit to follow even if there is no sleep problem.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: ● A healthy exercise schedule during the morning hours helps sleep. Te time of exercise should be preferably morning and best avoided just before sleep time. Te intensity of the exercise should be mild to moderate and never severe, especially if done during evening. Severe exercise can delay sleep in some insomnia patients, but a moderate to vigorous exercise schedule may be benefcial for OSA patients. Te vigorous exercise protocol, however, should be done only with the consultation of the physician and under supervision to avoid deleterious efects on the heart. Mild to moderate exercise done in the morning hours is found to advance sleep that evening. Patients with circadian rhythm disorder should be watched for their requirements, their biological day and night, and prescribed exercise as a lifestyle intervention.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: ● Food habits are important. Do not have very heavy meals before sleep time. Avoid lots of

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: fuids just before sleep time. Spicy foods cause trouble at night by causing refux, and foods rich in tyramine (e.g., cheese, bacon, etc.) cause problem sleeping and hence are best avoided. Warm milk is known to induce sleep due to the high tryptophan in it, and it relaxes the individual. A word of caution for patients with lactose intolerance and for those who cannot tolerate fuids: avoid milk near sleep time.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: ● Avoid long afernoon naps. A nap should not be more than 20–40 minutes. Frequent naps during the daytime are best avoided in the healthy population. In cases of advanced sleepwake disorders, naps may be benefcial to prescribe for these patients. Naps in these patients can help them perform better during the latter part of the day, especially if they are elderly. Te exact time of the nap needs consultation.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: Sleep education can be done using a 2-week sleep diary of the individual. Tis makes the interaction more individualized.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: Multicomponent CBTI is strongly recommended for the treatment of chronic insomnia in adults. When the initial side efects are seen to be due to sleep restriction, a gradual change in habits and cognitive restructuring has been found to show a higher beneft-to-harm ratio. However, in cases of comorbid medical or psychiatric conditions, the beneft-to-harm ratio must be considered before or during CBTI, and the therapist should be vigilant about the side efects. Cases where sleep restriction is to be avoided or sleep deprivation efects are not desired, clinician must keep a note of the beneft-to-harm ratio before advising CBTI.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: Multicomponent brief therapy for insomnia includes reduced CBT sessions, which may be only 1–4 in number, along with sleep restriction, stimulus control, and relaxation therapies. text: Lifestyle interventions based on principles for sleep disorders can include an exercise prescription and diet charts. A thought record can be done before going to bed to avoid carrying problems to bed before going to sleep. Exercises can be done specially for toning the neck muscles, facial muscles, and belly to help in obstructive sleep apnea. A well-timed exercise, exposure to sunlight or bright light, and maintaining social cues to promote good sleep can help in circadian rhythm disorders and might help insomniacs.

text: LIGHT AS A THERAPEUTIC OPTION

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: Te efect of light on circadian rhythm varies with the timing at which it is given. It has been found that if bright light is given before the body core temperature is minimum (CBTmin), it delays the sleep-wake cycle and that, if it is given afer the CBTmin, it advances the sleep cycle. So, in a normal sleep-wake cycle that is coordinated with light and dark phases, bright light exposure in the evening delays sleep and in the morning causes advancement in sleep at night. For artifcial means of
