chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: Light therapy is recommended by AASM for adults with advanced sleep-wake phase syndrome vs. no treatment and for elderly and dementia cases of irregular sleep-wake rhythm disorder. However, its use with melatonin is not recommended for elderly with dementia cases. Light therapy is also recommended for jet lag disorder and in shif work disorder patients.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: Delivery of light can be done from a natural source or by artifcial means. Te advantage of a natural source is the relative ease and the low cost, but the disadvantage—or rather the need for the artifcial means of delivery of light—is always the inaccessibility of the natural source at the time required. Te artifcial source can be given to the patient during nighttime too.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: Delivery of light by artifcial source involves the following requirements:

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: ● Te light should be oriented in such a way that it is presented to the individual from above, since the lower part of the retina has an enhanced efect on suppression of melatonin.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: ● Choosing the spectrum of light, with flters if required, the output intensity, the size of source, and the positioning of the irradiating surface needs to be decided. Glare should be reduced, and heat emission should not be uncomfortable. Te portability of the equipment, if required by the patient, determines the choice of the equipment.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: ● Artifcial sources of light can be:

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: ● A light box of a standard size of 2×4 feet kept on a table 3 feet away from the user.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: ● Fluorescent lamps or lights. For fuorescent lamps, the ballast frequency should be as per the requirement.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: ● Te light-generating device should be validated and conform to the standards for therapeutics.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: ● Te adverse efects of bright light therapy should always be kept in mind. Incandescent

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: lamps should never be used for light therapy as their illumination is harmful to the retinal pigment epithelium. Very small devices used for light therapy also are not advisable as a small change in head position can afect the amount of light reaching the retina and thus change the chronobiotic efect. Broad feld illumination is preferred and can even be given while the sleeper is sleeping as a dawn stimulation. Naturalistic dawn can be created with 250 lux of light intensity.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: ● Light therapy can be a problem in cases with a history of photosensitive medications; examples are drugs like phenothiazines, antimalarials, psoralen, etc. Retinopathy is an absolute contraindication for bright light therapy. Also, it may not be acceptable for patients with eye diseases and for some who experience light-therapy-related headaches. Constant supervision should be done of patients, and consultation of ophthalmologists or dermatologists may be considered before starting it and also during the treatment.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: Tere is an individual susceptibility to the efect of light on melatonin suppression, and hence individualized treatment under supervision is always recommended. Natural lighting is preferred for therapy. Exposure to light in the morning hours and avoidance to bright light before sleeping is one of the most inexpensive yet efective methods of light therapy.

chapter: 22 Sleep Hygiene Principles and Nonpharmacological Interventions including Light Therapy
text: A combination therapy using behavioral treatment using natural light exposure in the morning, following sleep hygiene principles, and postawakening light therapy has been found to show some therapeutic evidence, though weak for adults and children sufering from delayed sleep phase syndrome. For the use of light therapy in various circadian rhythm disorders, see Chapter 13.

chapter: 23 Identifying the Need for Counselling
text: A need to know when to send an individual for counselling becomes practically important for sleep problems for the simple reason of preventing further deterioration of the problem. Patients ofen go unnoticed because their telltale signs are missed during outpatient consultations by physicians who are not looking for them. Tis relative lack of proactiveness increases the patient burden on society. Te requirement of counselling needs to be picked up early so that it can be nipped in the bud, e.g., for college students or schoolchildren, a faint glimpse of a problem can be corrected faster and more permanently than when it is addressed afer many years of simmering inside, probably erupting into a full-blown disease or disorder.

text: WHAT IS COUNSELLING?

chapter: 23 Identifying the Need for Counselling
text: Counselling is a one-on-one method where a counsellor and the person seeking counselling, referred to as a counselee, interact in a nonthreatening, safe environment. “Safe” implies that this interaction happens because of mutual trust and faith developed between the counsellor and counselee. Terefore, it may take some time for the actual counselling session to be efective. Te objective of the counselling session is to enable the counselee to identify the problem and seek acceptance and self-direction. Te counselee fnds the way to fnd solutions to his or her problems and determines methods in which to overcome them. Note that merely providing information and giving advice is not considered counselling.

text: Robin: “I have been studying till late for my college exams. I go to bed at 12 midnight but am unable to sleep till 3 o’clock. Sometimes I toss and turn the entire night and feel I have been awake the entire night.”

text: “Oh . . . I see. So please tell me in detail. What do you do when you don’t get to sleep?” the counsellor quickly inquired.

text: Robin: “I keep thinking about my preparation, future or take my book and read till the time I start feeling asleep.”

text: “Do you mean to say you are worried about your future? And your anxiety makes you lose your sleep?” asked the counsellor.

text: Robin: “Maybe, how would I know?” “You tell me. Are you unduly worried about the exam? Do you get restless, jittery, anxious during daytime? Is your sleep disturbance greater when you are preoccupied or anxious? Tell me more about your life and routine,” the counsellor said.

text: Robin: “Actually, I have been a good student and wanted to get admission in medicine. My parents could not aford my entrance fees at the time, so I joined another course and apart from my studies, I started taking home tuitions for schoolchildren to make ends meet. text: HOW IS COUNSELLING DIFFERENT

chapter: 23 Identifying the Need for Counselling
text: FROM COGNITIVE BEHAVIORAL

chapter: 23 Identifying the Need for Counselling
text: THERAPY (CBT)?

chapter: 23 Identifying the Need for Counselling
text: In CBT, the therapist aims at working together with the individual on changing behavior and restructuring cognitively, i.e., modifying the thinking patterns and beliefs of the individual that hamper health. Counselling, on the other hand, helps the individual to identify the problem and formulate strategies to help cope with the issues. Here the counsellor makes Robin understand himself enough to fnd his own solutions and hopes that Robin follows them. It is less directive than CBT.

chapter: 23 Identifying the Need for Counselling
text: WHEN CAN ONE REFER FOR

chapter: 23 Identifying the Need for Counselling
text: COUNSELLING?

chapter: 23 Identifying the Need for Counselling
text: A timely counselling may ward of a brewing disorder/disease. Counselling may detect the problem at an early stage and may ofer a solution through simple lifestyle modifcation. Counselling for sleep-related issues should be a problem-based intervention and not an illness-based intervention. Many factors in routine life events can cause sleep disturbances without causing an illness, and the remedy for that can be simple and efective, with sleep-related counselling.

chapter: 23 Identifying the Need for Counselling
text: Counselling may be done by any health care worker trained in the basics of counselling. Counselling may be provided by a doctor who is treating an individual for an associated problem, such as a case of hypertension or diabetes with an

chapter: 23 Identifying the Need for Counselling
text: associated sleep disturbance. Also, a primary care physician might feel a need to refer for cognitive behavioral therapy but, due to a lack of availability of a trained counsellor in the vicinity, may ask the patient to go for counselling instead. Sometimes the patient needs “talk time” to vent about the problems and can fnd a solution as Robin did in our case. Hence identifying the need and referring to a counsellor may be the only thing required. Primary care physicians should use their clinical discretion, especially when there is lack of trained personnel for CBT or when it is not feasible for the patient to go to the therapist frequently because of time and money constraints. However, monitoring and regular follow-ups must be made by the physician, and the patient must not be lef on his or her own afer referral to the counsellor.

chapter: 23 Identifying the Need for Counselling
text: CONCLUSION

chapter: 23 Identifying the Need for Counselling
text: Counselling remains an important component of therapy, especially in patients sufering with sleep problems and sleep disorders. Identifying the need for counselling by parents, teachers, peers, employers, students, patients, doctors, therapists, psychologists, and others remains pivotal in identifying and accepting the issue so that an early measure may be planned and implemented. Evaluation of the planned strategy is also an important role of the counsellor, who can help refer the individual to the doctor or therapist or for further counselling sessions as the need may be.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: BZRAs are common drugs used for the treatment of insomnia. Tere are old GABA receptor modulators like temazepam, furazepam, and estazolam. Ten the newer BZRAs with a much diferent chemical structure interact with GABA receptors, namely zolpidem, zaleplon, eszopiclone, and quazepam. Benzodiazepines have better safety profles compared to drugs like barbiturates, which can cause respiratory depression, sedation, a coma-like state, or even death. Zolpidem is considered a safer medication to induce more physiologic sleep. It has only few withdrawal symptoms and is less likely to cause drug tolerance.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Effects on Sleep

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Benzodiazepine receptor antagonists can cause sedation, relieve anxiety, induce muscle relaxation, decrease sleep onset time, and cause amnesia. From the sleep architecture point of view, a decrease in initial sleep latency and an increase in total sleep time are the most efective advantages of losing these drugs. Tey decrease the stage N1 sleep and slow wave N3 sleep. Te N2 sleep amount is increased. Tese agents increase REM sleep latency and decrease total REM sleep time. Zolpidem, zaleplon, and eszopiclone do not have any efect on N3 slow wave sleep. Benzodiazepine receptor antagonist drugs are classifed according to their timing and duration of efect into short-acting, intermediate-acting, and long-acting medications.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Triazolam, Zolpidem, and Zaleplon

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: If a patient needs a second dose in the middle of the night to continue consolidated sleep, zaleplon is the drug of choice because of its rapid onset of action and shortest half-life compared to other drugs in this category. It has a short half-life of approximately 1 hour.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Clonazepam, quazepam, diazepam, and furazepam have a half-life of 23 hours, 39 hours, 43 hours, and 74 hours, respectively. Due to the extremely long half-lives, these are not the ideal drugs for treatment of insomnia as they are efective and can impair daytime functioning and have other side efects. However, they can be appropriately used in patients who have insomnia as well as daytime symptoms of anxiety and who need longacting anxiolytic therapy.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Clonazepam is considered the standard of therapy for the initial treatment of REM sleep behavior disorder. Its efcacy has been proven, and residual daytime impairment is minimal.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Rebound Insomnia

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: When discontinued, all the benzodiazepines are known to leave some degree of rebound insomnia. However, the newer benzodiazepine receptor agonists have less incidence of rebound insomnia. Due to the rapid turnover, short-acting benzodiazepines have a greater incidence of rebound insomnia compared to the longer-acting drugs. Rebound insomnia can also be dose dependent; that is, higher doses are likely to cause more chances of rebound insomnia compared to the lower doses of the medication. Of all the available drugs, zopiclone causes the lowest incidence of rebound insomnia. Longer-acting benzodiazepines, with a slow and gradual decline in their blood concentrations, do not cause rebound symptoms when they are withdrawn.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Tere are two types of melatonin receptors: MT 1 and MT 2. Ramelteon works on both. Currently, it has rapid onset of action and shortness to sleep latency, while increasing total sleep time. Most patients tolerate the drug well due to the low side efect profle. It should be carefully used in patients with liver disease as it is metabolized by the liver.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: TREATMENT OF INSOMNIA

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Insomnia and depression can coexist in approximately 60–70% of patients. About one-third of patients with chronic insomnia also developed depression. Insomnia can present 9 months prior to the clinical onset of major depression. Patients with chronic insomnia invariably develop depression. Many available pharmaceutical agents can address both insomnia and depression and should be considered in such a patient population.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Tricyclic antidepressant medications have anticholinergic and serotonergic properties. Tese medications are sedating, and the onset of the sedation efect is immediate. It takes several weeks for the antidepressant efect to occur. Obviously, these drugs also have a signifcant side efect profle due to their anticholinergic activity.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Trazodone

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Trazodone is an interesting medication that is considered the number one drug used by providers in the management of insomnia. Tis is a non-serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) antidepressant. Trazodone has anticholinergic, serotonergic, and noradrenergic properties. Its major side efects include cardiac arrhythmias, priapism, and orthostatic hypotension.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Mirtazapine has sedating properties along with the antidepressant efect. In some patients, appetite is also improved. It has been used in the treatment

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: While using the Tricyclic antidepressants, special attention should be given to the possibility of cardiac arrhythmias, orthostatic hypotension, dry mouth, urinary retention, and blurred vision. Tese efects can be life-threatening. Many other selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, including paroxetine, fuoxetine, and sertraline, have been used in patients with coexistent insomnia and depression. Combination therapy has been tried with antidepressants and benzodiazepines. Mild benzodiazepine improves the subjective quality of sleep and does not tend to interfere with the antidepressant efects. Short-acting benzodiazepines such as zaleplon or zolpidem should be considered for this purpose.

text: CNS Stimulants

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Currently the most common and relatively safer CNS stimulant is modafnil. However, methylphenidate, dextroamphetamine, or other historical stimulants have been used. Tese agents increase wakefulness and performance, as well as improve the sense of fatigue and tiredness.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Methylphenidate

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Methylphenidate increases sleep latency. It is a schedule II medication and needs a prescription. It has multiple side efects, including headaches, insomnia, nervousness, and akathisia, to mention a few.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Dextroamphetamine

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Dextroamphetamine is another stimulant that was historically used and is now used occasionally. It has multiple formulations and dosing frequencies. Its major side efects include psychotic behavior, insomnia, and cardiovascular complications.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Modafnil

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Modafnil is a rather recently introduced drug that is well tolerated and has mild to moderate side efects. It increases wakefulness during the daytime and reduces daytime sleepiness. It is given in the morning and therefore does not have

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders

text: any efect on nighttime sleep. Te most common side efect is headaches, which tend to resolve over time. GI irritation can also occur. Dose modifcations are needed in patients with liver disease and advanced age.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Combination Therapy

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Combination therapy is desirable, and the patients who have poor response to safer agents like modafnil. However, methylphenidate and dextroamphetamine can be added with increasing doses, and a well-designed titration is scheduled. At this time, the patient may be referred to a sleep specialist or psychiatrist with experience in the use of these drugs. Many psychiatric and psychological conditions like insomnia and psychosis can be precipitated by the long-term use of these medications. If side efects occur, the dose de-escalation should be attempted frst.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: SLEEP INTRUSIONS

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: REM sleep can include increased fullness, causing symptoms of sleep paralysis or cataplexy. Tricyclic antidepressants are commonly used drugs for managing cataplexy and sleep analysis. Many REM-suppressing medications, including tricyclic antidepressants and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, are used efectively for this purpose. Signifcant withdrawal and rebound symptoms can occur if these medications are suddenly stopped. Despite the potential side efects, tricyclic antidepressants are efective in most patients. If a patient is unable to tolerate the anticholinergic side efects, drugs like fuoxetine should be considered. Again, consider referring the patient to a sleep specialist if initial therapy begins to fail or if side efects begin to occur.

text: TREATMENT OF CENTRAL SLEEP

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: APNEA CAUSING INSOMNIA

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Central sleep apnea manifests as sleep maintenance insomnia. Many therapies have been attempted with variable success rates. While oxygen is used to stabilize ventilation by increasing PCO2 mildly, it may not work in severe cases. Oxygen therapy in the setting works by Haldane efect afects and blunts the hypoxic ventilatory drive. Another form

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: of central sleep apnea, Cheyne–Stokes breathing, occurs in patients with congestive heart failure and most commonly afer cerebrovascular accidents. It can be treated with Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, digoxin, diuretics, and beta blockade. Small studies have shown some efective role of methimazole since, adding dead space, acetazolamide, and a variety of positive-airwaypressure-delivered systems.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Methylxanthines

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: As previously noted, methylxanthines such as theophylline have been reported to improve central sleep apnea and the apnea-hypopnea index within 5 days of treatment in patients with Cheyne–Stokes respiration and congestive heart failure. However, from the primary care perspective, the patient should be referred for further evaluation and be managed by a sleep specialist.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Oxygen

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Oxygen by way of the Haldane efect is considered a stabilizer of the breathing pattern in patients with Cheyne–Stokes breathing. It is not known if the oxygen therapy improves daytime symptoms or cardiac performance. While there is much discussion regarding the increase of the dead space or current active therapy, such therapy is not commercially available. Exposure to carbon dioxide for therapeutic purposes is likely to be poorly tolerated and can cause disturbed sleep.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Acetazolamide

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Te mechanism of action of acetazolamide for use in central sleep apnea is not known. However, it is currently recommended by a few in the highaltitude central sleep apneas and similar medical conditions.

text: While drug therapy is not the frst line of therapy in the treatment of parasomnias, good sleep hygiene, avoiding sleep deprivation of any cause, avoidance of substance use, and the identifcation and management of underlying sleep disorders causing the parasomnia should be considered frst. Mild cases tend to improve with the passage

text: APNEA (OSA)

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: According to the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, the current position of pharmaceutical treatment for obstructive sleep apnea is not optimal. However, pharmaceuticals can be efective as a secondary line of therapy to support positive airway pressure therapy: in this regard, protriptyline, nasal steroids, hormone replacement therapy, and modafnil.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Protriptyline

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: A number of studies particularly showed variable efcacy in the treatment of obstructive sleep apnea. Selective serotonin rehab uptake inhibitors have also been tested, but no recommendations are available at this time for use of either protriptyline or any selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRI) for the treatment of obstructive sleep apnea.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Nasal Steroids

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Nasal steroid sprays tend to work by reducing the airway obstruction by relieving the congestion of the nasal passage to the airfow. It is also useful for the patient of nasal CPAP who has allergies and other causes of nasal congestion.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Hormone Replacement Therapy

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Some studies, including a sleep heart health study, have documented the lower incidence of obstructive sleep apnea. However, currently there is no specifc recommendation regarding the use of hormone replacement therapy in the management of obstructive sleep apnea.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Modafnil has been evaluated as an adjunct to CPAP in patients who remain sleepy while being treated with CPAP. It is important to note that this application is limited to those who are actually using and compliant with CPAP.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Sleepwalking is a form of parasomnia as previously discussed. Te frst line of treatment for the same sleepwalking is identifcation and avoidance of the precipitating causes and securing a safe living space. Safety measures include fre safety, injury due to sharp objects, and locking the door and the windows. In severe cases where the patient is a danger to self or others, some recommendations regarding benzodiazepines and tricyclic antidepressants are available. However, primary care providers should refer these cases to the subspecialist management.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: SLEEP TERROR (ST)

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Sleep terrors tend to resolve over time, especially in the children. However, if sleep terrors are present in adulthood, it can be a signifcant problem that needs to be addressed by a sleep specialist, psychologist, or psychiatrist. Clonazepam, trazodone, and paroxetine have been reported to be useful. Again, the primary care provider should consider referring for subspecialty management.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: NIGHTMARES

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Nightmares are treated only if they are severely refractory. Since nightmares tend to occur during REM sleep, SSRI or tricyclic antidepressant therapy may be useful for REM suppression and therefore the potential decrease in the frequency of nightmares. Unresponsive cases should be referred for subspecialty consultation and management.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: REM BEHAVIOR DISORDER (RBD)

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: REM behavior disorder is a condition when the patients begin to act out their dreams. In most dreams, patients tend to fght an animal predator while trying to save and defend themselves. However, in sleep behavior, they start acting out the fght and hit the bed partner in the process, causing signifcant injuries. Clonazepam has been considered the frst-line medication recommended in most cases. Clonazepam should be considered carefully for patients with kidney problems, respiratory problems, severe liver disease, and glaucoma. Clonazepam should be gradually withdrawn if it has to be discontinued to avoid undesirable

text: RESTLESS LEG SYNDROME (RLS)

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Ropinirole or Pramipexole

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: RLS is a common condition frequently encountered in primary care practice. Dopamine agonists like ropinirole or pramipexole are the frst-line treatment. While gabapentin is the secondary therapy, opioids are used in certain patient populations. Benzodiazepines have been used with some success in a few cases.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: Dopaminergic Medications

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: LEVODOPA Levodopa, while short-acting, can be very efective in resolving RLS symptoms. Te real-life disadvantage of levodopa is augmentation, that is, the worsening of symptoms, their increasing intensity and spread to other areas of the body earlier in the day. Augmentation can afect up to 80% of the patients treated with levodopa. Te other problem, which can be severe, is rebound; that is, the symptoms tend to occur in the early morning hours and are more intense. Approximately 20–25% patients developed rebound phenomena.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: DOPAMINE AGONISTS Dopamine agonists are currently recommended therapy for the symptomatic control of the RLS. Tey have much less risk of the augmentation, but the risk of tolerance is high. Pramipexole improves the subjective symptoms of RLS and also improves periodic limb movements while awake. Ropinirole has similar efcacy and is considered the frst-line therapy. Rotigotine is another medication used for the same purpose but has signifcant side efects in susceptible individuals. Apomorphine has been used with fair success in patients with RLS.

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: ANTICONVULSANTS Although the mechanism of action of gabapentin in the treatment of RLS is not known, they are the second-line treatment for the patient intolerant to dopamine agonist. It is more efective in patients with renal failure who are dependent on dialysis. Carbamazepine has been efective in some

chapter: 24 Pharmacological Agents Used in Various Sleep Disorders
text: OPIOIDS Finally, opioids are commonly used in the treatment of RLS even when they are considered the third line of treatment. Many patients are intolerant to dopamine agonists and may not be suitable candidates for gabapentin-like medications. Propoxyphene and oxycodone have been used successfully. In addition, methadone does not reduce RLS symptoms. More suitable candidates for methadone therapy would be patients who are poorly responsive to dopamine agonist therapy. Methadone therapy also does not cause augmentation. Long-acting benzodiazepine clonazepam has been successfully used in few patients with RLS.

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances
text: Positional therapy treats individuals who sleep in the supine position, causing the obstruction of the airway and leading to a spectrum of symptoms from snoring to obstructive events. A variety of methods are available to avoid assuming the supine position. A night shirt with a back pocket containing a tennis ball, commercially made vests, specially designed pillows, positional alarms, and verbal instructions have been recommended. Multiple studies have demonstrated improvement in intensity, frequency, snoring rate, or duration of the snoring or of obstructive events while using such therapeutic devices. Studies of patients with obstructive sleep apnea have also demonstrated

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances
text: A review of the compliance rate with positional therapy indicated that, depending on the type of therapy chosen, the patient may not be able to use the device as recommended. Te reasons are discomfort and tightness of the vest around the chest, restless sleep, frequent awakenings, sweating during the night, and inability to resume the preferred and favored sleep position. A few studies have documented lack of efectiveness, back pain, and lack of improvement in the quality of sleep or daytime sleepiness. Not all patients learned to avoid the supine position and either needed continued use or periodic training for reinforcement. Most attended full-night sleep studies called polysomnography (PSG), by which the supine and nonsupine AHI was calculated as a guide in the decision to recommend positional therapy.

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances
text: Combination therapy for the treatment of obstructive sleep apnea, including continuous positive airway pressure and surgical interventions, according to a few case reports and a small series of reports, suggests that additional positional therapy signifcantly improved the response to treatment with surgical intervention like uvelopalatopharyngoplasty.

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances
text: In addition, positional therapy has been evaluated in combination with oral appliance therapy. Patients with position-dependent obstructive sleep apnea receiving positional therapy along with the oral appliance are noted to be more responsive to oral appliance therapy. Reduction in the severity of the obstructive events in the supine position was noted to be the strongest protection of successful combination therapy.

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances
text: Compliance with the CPAP therapy is relatively poor, and one of the reasons is noted to be high intolerable CPAP pressures. Combination therapy with positional devices has shown a reduction in the required positive pressure to open up the airway and make the CPAP therapy more tolerable. At least one study showed that the compliance in fact improved with the auto-CPAP therapy and that the patient also used a positional device.

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances
text: As previously noted, commercial products are available that utilize a snowball. Such devices consist of the placement of a number of balls in a pouch attached to the back of the sleepwear. Te presence of the ball becomes uncomfortable in the supine position and forces the patient to return to the nonsupine position. Such devices can be handmade at home and could be an inexpensive and easy to use alternative. Sleep position monitors work like a loud alarm if the patient turns on the back. Multiple similar products are available commercially. Products like nasal strips and throat sprays are not the subject of this chapter; however, these are freely available and have variable efects on patients’ sleep.

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances
text: Overall, appliances are considered frst-line therapy for mild to moderate obstructive sleep apnea, just like positive airway pressure. Tey are also considered in cases of severe sleep apnea when the patient is unable to tolerate and refuses treatment

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances
text: with positive airway pressure devices. Oral appliances are not known to be superior to the diferent forms of upper airway surgery and seem to be more efcacious. While oral appliances are well tolerated and have a slightly better side efect profle, the efcacy compared to positive airway pressure in the correction of the apnea-hypopnea index is lower. If the disease continues to get worse and takes a severe form or if body weight increases, the efcacy of the oral appliance can decrease. Most of the side efects are minor and can be easily managed.

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances
text: Types of Oral Appliances

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances
text: Oral appliances have been used for the treatment of sleep disordered breathing since 1983. Initial oral appliances also used tongue-retaining devices along with mandibular advancement devices. At this time, a number of user-friendly designs have been developed. Multiple diferent oral appliances are available, and currently 30 appliances have the approval of the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances
text: Few appliances are approved for snoring only. Te oral appliances work by a mechanism where they open the airway by lifing and moving tongue away from the posterior oropharynx and advancing the jaw forward to create more space in the oropharyngeal area. While two basic types of appliances are used, the more common are the mandibular advancement devices, also known as the oral appliances. Te tongue-retaining device works by application of suction on the tongue with the pull forward so that it cannot fall back and block the airway. Tis appliance is not as popular as the manual advancement device/oral appliance.

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances
text: Mandibular advancement devices are the more common and popular equipment. Recommended devices are custom made, two-piece devices that are attached by a hinge. Tis device covers the dental arches and forms a rigid monoblock when closed together. Diferent designs include an icing assembly, hook, strap, wire, or rod to hold the two pieces together. Such a tile design allows the movement of the lower jaw and provides anterior-posterior and occasionally vertical adjustment fexibility.

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances
text: A few appliances cover only the upper jaw and teeth with a ramp-like portion that extends over the tongue and reaches inferiorly behind the maxillary incisors. When the mouth closes, the mandibular teeth make contact with the ramp and guide the mandible forward as it closes. Tese

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances
text: appliances are only efective if a patient sleeps with the mouth closed.

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances
text: Tongue-retaining devices are made out of sof medical-grade silicone and look like a bulb or cavity. Te tongue is pushed inside the bulb, which sticks to the tongue. Te bulb can also be slightly squeezed in position on the tongue and then released to create a suction force so that it stays attached to the tongue. Te suction device can be really helpful in edentulous patients. According to the studies, tongue-retaining devices are not as efective as oral appliances. Patients are also more intolerant to these devices.

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances
text: Mechanism of Oral Appliances

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances
text: It is not known how the oral appliances work in opening the airway. It is, however, suspected that the inability to change the current position and therefore increase the oropharyngeal space is the likely mechanical mechanism. It is well-known that sleep disordered breathing occurs at the level of the oropharynx as the most common site of obstruction. Due to the oral appliance’s efect on the tongue, as well as the inability to hold the mandible forward, increases the upper airway volume and stabilizes the pharyngeal dilator muscles to decrease the collapsibility of the pharynx. Many people believe that oral appliances increase tone in the genioglossus muscle (the tongue), which also helps to reduce the collapsibility of the pharynx.

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances
text: Effcacy of Oral Appliances

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances
text: Te current efcacy of the oral appliances is considered to be variable from mild to severe obstructive sleep apnea. It ranges between 76 and 40%, respectively. According to the dental literature, the overall 1 year rate of success as measured by reduction in the apnea-hypopnea index to less than 10 events per hour is found to be 54%. Complete resolution of the apnea-hypopnea index to less than 5 events per hour is noted in approximately 37% of the patients. Oral appliances lower the apneahypopnea index and oxygen desaturation events.

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances
text: Compliance with Oral Appliances

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances
text: Interestingly, however, compliance with the use of oral appliances is variable from 48 to 84%. Tese data ranges over 1 year as long-term compliance

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances
text: data are not available. It is suspected that, with the continued use over time, the rate of compliance will go down. According to patient experience, there are multiple reasons for the lower compliance that include discomfort at the jaw, lack of perceived efcacy, or changing over to positive airway pressure therapy. It is also noticed that regular users tend to adjust to the appliances and have less incidence of side efects compared to known users.

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances
text: Side Effects of Oral Appliances

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances
text: While compared to positive airway pressure therapy, oral appliances are supposed to be better tolerated; however, minor side efects and complications are experienced by most patients. Te complications are transient and improve upon removal of the appliance and tend to become more tolerable over time. Common side efects include temporomandibular joint discomfort, muscle pain, dry mouth, drooling, teeth movement, and soreness. Bite changes can occur and can especially be felt in the morning afer removal of the appliance. Tese appliances can also cause a posterior open bite that is defned as the inability to close on the back teeth. Since oral appliances work by the forward movement of the mandible throughout the night, other teeth are able to contact but back teeth are lef open. Various mechanisms are considered implicating the efect of the lateral pterygoid muscle or alterations in the temporomandibular joint capsule. Again, these changes are reversible within a short time afer removal of the implants. Still, 10–15% of the patients will sufer with persistent and occasionally pulmonary changes. If complications are severe, then corrections can be made by orthodontic intervention, restorative dentistry, and surgical interventions.

chapter: 25 Simple Positional Devices, Dental Appliances
text: Considering all this, it must be realized that oral appliances provide an alternative to positive airway pressure therapy and prevent the complications related to obstructive sleep apnea. Tis risk-vs.-beneft ratio should be discussed with the patient so that he can be encouraged to continue using therapy for obstructive sleep apnea.

chapter: 26 Titration Protocols, Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP), and Other PAP Devices
text: BiPAP therapy provides two diferent levels of pressure. During inspiration, a high level of pressure applied to open the airway is known as inspiratory positive airway pressure (IPAP); during exhalation, the patient is allowed to breathe out again at a lower pressure, known as expiratory positive airway pressure (EPAP). Te diference between the two pressures is the pressure support. Tis pressure keeps the airway open throughout the respiratory cycle. Despite this improvement, BiPAP therapy has not been proven to be more acceptable to the patient population, and compliance has remained the same. Multiple BiPAP systems have been introduced with unique proprietary features in order to manipulate the application of pressure or the fow to increase patient comfort.

Te pressure relief is calculated by many parameters including patient efort and the airfow and is variable from one breath to the other. At least 2–3 diferent levels of pressure relief options are available according to the patient’s comfort. Tese algorithms are proprietary and are variable among diferent brands of the equipment.

text: In an initial nonrandomized study that followed 89 CPAP-naive OSAS patients over a 3 month period, patients using the C-Flex technology demonstrated improved compliance compared with those using fxed-pressure CPAP therapy. In fact, after 3 months of treatment, compliance with C-Flex therapy was greater by an average of 1.7 hours per night. Subjective sleepiness and objective outcomes were similar between the groups. While these initial results were intriguing, the study was limited by its nonrandomized design.

chapter: 26 Titration Protocols, Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP), and Other PAP Devices
text: A randomized control trial of C-Flex technology evaluated 52 CPAP-naive patients with newly diagnosed OSAS and allocated them to either fxed CPAP or C-Flex therapy. All patients in the C-Flex group were treated with a C-Flex setting of 3. After 7 weeks of treatment, both CPAP and C-Flex groups demonstrated equal objective compliance (5.2 and 5.3 hours, respectively). Both treatments also demonstrated equal improvements in subjective daytime sleepiness and reductions in the AHI. Finally, C-Flex therapy offered no signifcant benefts in that subgroup of patients who required pressures of ≥9 cm H2O.
